paper_title: Fast and Exact Relative-Position Attention via Structure-Aware Kernels

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Relative-position attention mechanisms offer compelling alternatives to RoPE across various transformer architectures, delivering superior performance in domains such as audio. These mechanisms typically modify attention scores by adding content-position or bias-position terms. Unlike RoPE, which encodes position via per-token rotations directly on the queries and keys, relative-position terms generally require pairwise offset-dependent computation or lookups, complicating their integration into fused attention kernels and introducing severe memory, bandwidth, and compute overheads as sequences scale. To address this bottleneck, we propose an exact attention algorithm that incorporates additive relative-position terms into FlashAttention-style tiled computation. Our method (1) uses offset-aware tiling to avoid redundant indexing and memory accesses, (2) computes only the necessary key/query-relation products and reuses them across token pairs in both forward and backward passes, and (3) uses offset-based gradient sharding and aggregation, eliminating atomic contention. We provide a unified, efficient Triton implementation across diverse relative-position attention mechanisms and evaluate it against naive and specialized implementations. For 8K-token sequences, our method speeds up the forward (backward) pass by 1.8-6.4$\times$ (2.0-21$\times$) and reduces peak memory up to 2.9-128$\times$ (1.4-54$\times$) over the strongest baseline for each mechanism, enabling long-context end-to-end transcription that is 1.8$\times$ faster and uses 2.4$\times$ less memory. Our method thus provides a drop-in, hardware-efficient solution for scaling relative-position attention transformers.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: The Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017) has revolutionized modern machine learning, from large language models (LLMs) in natural language processing to foundation models in speech, vision, and biology. At its core is the scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) mechanism, which allows input tokens to directly attend to each other and aggregate mutual information. However, scaling these models to larger inputs introduces two fundamental challenges, namely injecting scalable positional information into the network, and keeping the computation and memory footprint of SDPA tractable despite its quadratic complexity. For standard content-based attention, IO-aware kernels such as FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022; Dao, 2024) resolved the quadratic memory bottleneck by streaming blocks of tokens through fast on-chip SRAM, avoiding the materialization of the full score matrix in GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM). Paired with parameter-free, token-wise rotary position embeddings (RoPE) (Su et al., 2024), which can be seamlessly integrated into fused kernels, this pipeline now serves as the backbone of most autoregressive LLMs. 1INSAIT, Sofia University St. Kliment Ohridski. Correspondence to: Delyan Boychev <delyan.boychev@insait.ai>. Preprint. Under review. Relative-position attention Parameter-free positional encodings, such as RoPE and ALiBi (Press et al., 2022), are not without drawbacks. Despite their computational efficiency, they often fail to use context beyond the sequence lengths seen during training (Kazemnejad et al., 2023; Hua et al., 2025), where learned relative biases such as T5s generalize better (Kazemnejad et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024). Consequently, learnable relative-position encodings remain an enticing alternative for Transformer models. This class of mechanisms additively augments attention scores with learnable terms that depend on the relative distance between query and key tokens, either through content-to-position projections or scalar biases. This allows modeling explicit, shift-invariant relationships across sequences, and has remained enticing for speech models (Barrault et al., 2023; Sekoyan et al., 2025; Abouelenin et al., 2025), text encoding (He et al., 2023; Zaratiana et al., 2025), proteomics (Elnaggar et al., 2022), and genomics (Linder et al., 2025). Efficiency limitations of relative-position attention Despite their modeling advantages, relative-position attention mechanisms are largely incompatible with standard fused attention kernels. (d) One thread block per query tile sums gradients on chip, avoiding atomic contention. . (c) Each shared entry signed to eliminate. Programmable attention frameworks such as FlexAttention (Dong et al., 2025) offer partial solution by fusing user-defined per-score callbacks and enabling limited precomputation; however, they still suffer from redundant computation, repeated memory lookups, and atomic contention during backpropagation. Lacking efficient kernels, practitioners often resort to replacing relativeposition encodings entirely and retraining models from scratch, as seen in Flashzoi (Hingerl et al., 2025) and FlashSwin (Kataria et al., 2026), or switch to RoPE-based alternatives such as ModernBERT (Warner et al., 2025). Our work To address these limitations, we introduce an exact algorithm for relative-position mechanisms. Rather than treating pairwise offsets as opaque per-element lookups, our method exploits the block-level structure of relative distances across the attention matrix (Fig. 1a). Specifically, our method projects queries and keys only onto the offset ranges reachable within each token block (Fig. 1b), structures tile traversal around constantand variable offset regions to maximize data reuse and avoid redundant indexing (Fig. 1c), and shards backward gradient accumulation by offset to eliminate atomic contention entirely (Fig. 1d). Empirically, our method substantially reduces both runtime and memory consumption across forward and backward passes in production speech and text models. Our kernels significantly outperform generalist and specialized implementations, as well as state-of-the-art frameworks such as FlexAttention, FlashAttention-4 (Zadouri et al., 2026), and FlashInfer (Ye et al., 2025), even when those frameworks are augmented with our preprojected relation decomposition. In particular, for 8K-token sequences, our method beats the strongest baseline for each mechanism by 1.86.4 in the forward pass and 2.021 in the backward pass, while reducing peak memory usage by 2.9128 and 1.454, respectively. Applied end-to-end to long-context speech transcription, it delivers 1.8 speedup and 2.4 lower memory consumption on Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 (Sekoyan et al., 2025), enabling significantly more efficient deployment and training. Key contributions Our main contributions include: unified formulation of additive relative-position attention spanning four mechanisms, exposing shared structure amenable to kernel-level optimization. An exact, drop-in tiled algorithm for fast and memoryefficient relative-position attention. High-performance implementations of our method, validated against high-precision reference, and comprehensive evaluations across diverse model architectures, sequence lengths, and NVIDIA GPU architectures.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: In this section, we describe relevant prior work on optimizing standard attention and programmable backends for non-standard attention mechanisms. We then describe the uses of relative-position attention and their limitations due to the lack of general optimization algorithms.

sections.title: 2.1 Optimizing Standard Attention
sections.content: Modern Transformer architectures rely on scaled dotproduct attention (SDPA) (Vaswani et al., 2017). However, naive implementations materialize the full attention score and probability matrices in high-bandwidth memory (HBM), incurring storage and I/O costs that grow quadratically with sequence length. To mitigate this bottleneck, Milakov & Fast and Exact Relative-Position Attention via Structure-Aware Kernels Gimelshein (2018) introduced an online softmax formulation that processes inputs in column-wise chunks, enabling exact attention computation in sub-quadratic memory (Rabe & Staats, 2021). FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022) combines this with IO-aware tiling in on-chip memory, recomputing attention tiles during the backward pass instead of storing large intermediate matrices. FlashAttention-2 (Dao, 2024) restructures the schedule to improve parallelism and reduce overhead by parallelizing the forward pass over query blocks and the backward pass over key blocks. FlashAttention-3 and -4 (Shah et al., 2024; Zadouri et al., 2026) further specialize this pipeline for newer GPUs. Existing kernels target content-based attention and cannot fuse learnable relative-position terms or their gradients. Our method bridges this gap by extending tiled execution to relative-position attention by restricting projections to reachable offsets, reusing them on constant-offset tiles, and using two-pass backward schedule (Triton Contributors, 2024) for atomic-free gradient accumulation.

sections.title: 2.2 Programmable and Specialized Backends
sections.content: To support attention variants without hand-writing kernel per model, recent frameworks expose programmable interfaces that preserve FlashAttentions optimizations. FlexAttention (Dong et al., 2025) compiles user-defined mask predicates and elementwise score modifications into fused tiled kernels, automatically deriving their backward pass. FlashInfer (Ye et al., 2025), AttentionEngine (Chen et al., 2025), and Flashlight (You et al., 2025) provide similar customization through templates or compilers, while others target variant families such as sparse masks (Wang et al., 2025) or low-rank biases (Wu et al., 2025). Because these frameworks express score modifications as pointwise callbacks on querykey pairs, they can only support relative-position terms via elementwise lookups into precomputed tables. Because this abstraction hides the tile structure, it cannot exploit spatial locality across constantoffset pairs, leading to redundant memory accesses during the forward pass and contention-heavy atomic additions (Dong et al., 2025) during gradient accumulation.

sections.title: 2.3 Relative-Position Attention
sections.content: Applications of relative-position attention While modern autoregressive language models largely rely on fixed positional schemes like RoPE (Su et al., 2024) and ALiBi (Press et al., 2022) that integrate neatly into standard SDPA kernels, many domains benefit from expressive, learnable relative-position encodings that inject pairwise token distances directly into the attention logits. Introduced by Shaw et al. (2018), this approach projects queries onto learned embeddings of clipped relative offsets. TransformerXL (Dai et al., 2019) expands this notion by incorporating unclipped offsets with learned query biases, DeBERTa (He et al., 2021; 2023) by modelling both content-to-position and position-to-content interactions, and T5 (Raffel et al., 2020) by mapping offsets to learned scalar bucket biases. Today, these mechanisms remain foundational for longcontext modeling across speech, text, and biology. They support the backbone of conformer-based (Gulati et al., 2020) speech and multimodal models such as Parakeet, Canary, SeamlessM4T v2, and Phi-4-multimodal (Sekoyan et al., 2025; Barrault et al., 2023; Abouelenin et al., 2025), DeBERTa-based text and extraction pipelines (Zaratiana et al., 2025), and biological sequence models in proteomics and genomics (Elnaggar et al., 2022; Avsec et al., 2021; Linder et al., 2025). Our method unifies the common computational patterns across all these architectures, providing single hardware-efficient algorithm. Optimizing relative-position attention Despite their widespread adoption, these architectures remain difficult to scale due to the overhead of computing and applying relative-position terms. Early implementations reduced the cost of positional projections by evaluating queryand key-relation dot products once per unique offset, and then mapping the resulting table via explicit index lookups (He et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2021) or row-shifting reshape operations (Huang et al., 2019; Dai et al., 2019). However, both strategies still materialize dense quadratic bias matrix in HBM. Subsequent systems have attempted to fuse this pipeline, though they remain either incomplete or model-specific. For instance, TensorRTs DeBERTa plugin (NVIDIA, 2022) and NeMos TransformerXL path (Kuchaiev et al., 2019) fuse the offset-gather step yet still materialize the full score matrix in HBM. On the other hand, FlashDeBERTa (Knowledgator, 2025) and GLiNER4j (Gravitee, 2026) integrate positional terms directly into tiled FlashAttention-style kernels (the latter for inference only), but are strictly tailored to DeBERTa. Lacking general kernel support, practitioners often modify and retrain the model instead: Flashzoi (Hingerl et al., 2025) replaces relative-position encodings with RoPE, with analogous replacements appearing for speech recognition (Zhang et al., 2025) and proposed for vision Transformers (Kataria et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026). Others turn to kernelized attention to incorporate relative positions in sub-quadratic time (Luo et al., 2021; Liutkus et al., 2021), but sacrificing exactness, which has unclear performance impact. Our method accelerates both training and inference across the full family of relative-position architectures without compromising model fidelity or numerical exactness.

sections.title: 3.3 Limitations of Existing Attention Backends
sections.content: Existing implementations gather or shift copies of the relative-position terms into dense square matrix before the softmax. Specifically, eager implementations follow one of two strategies, both of which reintroduce quadratic HBM bottlenecks. Naive implementations instantiate aQ ϕ(i,j) for every (i, j) pair, costing O(N 2d) work and O(N 2d) workspace. Preprojected implementations instead compute Q, RN in O(N Rd) work and O(N R) space, then gather or shift them into an bias matrix. Even with tiling instead of the bias, the precomputed tables require O(N R) storage, which often include unreachable columns (wasting compute and memory), fetches the same entry multiple times (e.g., when offsets are clipped), and remains quadratic for identity maps. In the backward pass, tiled execution faces an additional many-to-one reduction bottleneck in Eq. (6). Whenever multiple pairs (i, j) map to the same row = ϕ(i, j), up to O(N ) keys per query and O(N 2) pairs overall, their score gradients τ dSij must be summed into the same dZ ir, dZ jr, and dbr entries, causing severe atomic contention when accumulated via per-pair updates. While programmable backends such as FlexAttention can avoid the dense bias through fused per-score callbacks, scalar callback only sees single (i, j) pair at time. It cannot change how outer projections are allocated, reuse entries across tile of pairs sharing the same row r, or coordinate gradient ownership in backward to avoid atomic additions. Our method overcomes all of these bottlenecks with its relationaware tiled approach. Derivation of all equations is given in App. B.

sections.title: 4.3.3 Implementation
sections.content: We implement our method in Triton (Tillet et al., 2019) as drop-in replacement for relative-position attention, with adapters for Hugging Face and NeMo models that require no weight modifications. Each call dispatches kernel specialized at compile time to the active relation terms, map type and , masking, sequence packing, dropout, precision, and tile sizes, avoiding runtime branching and any overhead from disabled terms. Tile sizes are selected by sequencelength bucket from lookup tables tuned offline per GPU architecture, falling back to hardware resource heuristic when no table entry exists. Similarly, the saturation check (lines 1112 of Algorithm 1) splits each tiles inner loop into three contiguous ranges on the host rather than branching per tile. Sequence lengths remain runtime arguments so lengths within bucket share compiled kernels, with an optional precompilation step to warm the compiler cache. Users can trade compute for memory by selecting whether the forward pass saves and in HBM or recomputes them during backpropagation. sections.title: 5 EVALUATION
sections.content: In this section, we present the empirical evaluation of our method. We first describe our experimental setup, including the target mechanisms and hardware, alongside the baselines we compare against (5.1). We then evaluate our method at two levels. At the attention-block level we benchmark forward and backward throughput and memory footprints (5.2). Second, we apply our method in end-to-end tasks, including training and inference, while comparing downstream task quality across three production workloads (5.3). Finally, we isolate and measure the impact of each algorithmic optimization of our method in ablation studies (5.4).

sections.title: 5.4 Ablation Studies
sections.content: To isolate the efficacy of each part of our contribution, Table 7 switches off one component of our method at time, and registers the memory and efficiency tradeoff. App. further reports the results on every mechanism and the HBM traffic. Two methods carry most of the speedup. Without atomicfree gradients, the backward pass is 2.94.4 slower, needs 1.82.6 the memory, and loses determinism. The decomposition engines use atomics, hence their backward gap in 5.2. Without projections, every tile computes its own relation products, which slows the forward pass by 2.02.9 and the backward pass even more, but needs only 0.19 0.43 the memory, the same tradeoff GLiNER4j makes. The other methods are more targeted, with considerable gains of up to 1.3 in time or 1.5 in memory on the maps they serve  (Table 10)  . Reachable ranges save memory, mainly on TXLs identity map, while constant-range reuse speeds up the clipped and bucketed maps. Bucket copies add further speed at memory cost. Finally, recomputing the projections instead of retaining them cuts memory to 0.420.50 for 1.1 slowdown, which is how our method is able to fit Canarys longest windows (5.3).

sections.title: 6 LIMITATIONS
sections.content: While our method resolves the main bottlenecks of relativeposition attention, several limitations remain. First, identity maps such as Transformer-XLs assign distinct relation row to every offset, so their projection work and space remain quadratic in sequence length. Computing the projections inside each tile instead makes the space linear but is 2.0 2.9 slower in the forward pass  (Table 7)  . Second, maps whose relation rows do not cover consecutive offsets fall back to FP32 atomic accumulation, which is slower and not deterministic, although every evaluated mechanism avoids it. Third, our method favors generality across mechanisms, maps, and GPUs over hardware specialization. It autotunes its tile sizes but uses no architecture-specific primitives such as warp specialization or asynchronous bulk transfers (Shah et al., 2024; Zadouri et al., 2026), which could yield further speedups and which we leave as future work.

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented an exact tiled algorithm that unifies and accelerates additive relative-position attention. By restricting relation projections to reachable ranges, reusing entries across constant-offset tiles, and accumulating gradients by offset without atomics, our method removes the dense bias of existing backends, with its memory and bandwidth costs, and keeps gradients deterministic for identity, clipped, and bucketed maps. Across mechanisms and GPUs, our method is drop-in replacement for long-context training and inference in production models, so these mechanisms no longer need to be substituted for efficiency. sections.title: C KERNEL AND ALGORITHM DETAILS
sections.content: 4.3.3 summarizes our implementation. Here, we detail how our method maps Algorithms 1 and 2 onto kernels, how it reduces the relation gradients deterministically, how it stores relation projections in half precision, and which inputs and tile sizes its kernels support. Kernel structure Table 9 lists the kernels of our method in launch order, with the lines of Algorithms 1 and 2 that each one runs. The forward pass first projects every query group and key group onto its reachable range and stores the preprojected relation entries in HBM. The attention kernel then runs the tiled loop and writes and L. The backward pass computes and runs the query-parallel pass, whose gradient entries are reduced into dQ, dAQ, and db before the key-parallel pass starts. Both passes can therefore write their gradient entries into the same buffer. The key-parallel pass and its reduction then produce dK, dV , and dAK. If the forward pass does not save and K, the backward pass recomputes them with the projection kernel before it starts. When both AQ and are present, the projection kernel adds into the stored Q, so each score reads two entries instead of three. Bucket copies (line 1) run before the projection and copy the rows of the tables rather than the columns of the projections, AQ = EAQ, which gives the same = Q( AQ) = QE. Deterministic table gradients Each table gradient is sum over all tokens. Our method splits the tokens into chunks and computes dAQ = (cid:80) )Qc, and likewise dAK and db, in two kernels. In the first, each thread block computes the term of one chunk and writes it to HBM in FP32. In the second, these terms are summed in fixed order. For bucketed maps, the gradients of the copied rows are then summed back into their buckets, dAQ = Ed AQ, also in fixed order. No gradient is accumulated atomically, c(dZ so the backward pass is deterministic. Atomic fallback Accumulating gradients by offset (4.2) requires each relation row to cover one contiguous interval of offsets. This holds for identity, clipped, and bucketed maps, and our method checks it once per map on the host. Maps that fail it fall back to kernels that accumulate their relation gradients with FP32 atomic additions. Examples are maps that give δ and δ the same row, or maps that depend on more than the offset. Half-precision numerics Inputs may be in FP16, BF16, or FP32. The online softmax uses base-2 exponentials, with log2 folded into τ , and its statistics, the accumulators, and the boundary sums stay in FP32 on chip. In HBM, the gradient entries use the input precision. The relation projections use FP16 for both FP16 and BF16 inputs. BF16 gives up three mantissa bits for wider range, so FP16 stores the projections with an eight times smaller rounding error. For BF16 inputs, the projections are clamped to the FP16 range of 65504, so that an outlier cannot overflow to infinity. Masks, packing, and dropout The kernels support padding masks, causal masks, and packed variable-length sequences, in which each thread block processes query tile of one sequence. Attention dropout draws its mask from counter-based random number generator inside the kernels, so the backward pass regenerates the mask of the forward pass instead of storing it. Specialization and tuning The sequence-length buckets end at 64, 128, 384, 512, 768, 1K, 2K, 4K, and 8K tokens, and longer sequences use the 8K bucket. Besides the specializations of 4.3.3, each kernel is compiled separately for lengths that are and are not multiple of 16, so bucket needs at most two compilations per kernel. For multiples of 16, Triton can use wider memory accesses, so our model adapters pad each sequence to multiple of 16 tokens and mask the padding. For the same reason, each groups range of projection columns starts and ends on multiple of 16. Our lookup tables cover compute capabilities 8.0, 8.6, and 9.0 (A100, RTX A6000, and H100 or H200), with one entry per kernel, precision, head dimension, bucket, and set of relation terms. The hardware resource heuristic starts from 64 64 tile and shrinks it until its estimated registers and shared memory fit the GPU. Instead of both, our method can autotune each kernel at run time over short list of candidate tile sizes, once per bucket. All measurements in 5 use autotuning, which the end-to-end runs complete in the precompilation step before timing. The exception is the ablation that computes the projections inside each tile  (Table 7)  , which uses its fastest fixed tile sizes. sections.content: Kernel benchmarks forward pass is credited 4BHN 2d FLOPs for its two attention GEMMs plus 2BHN Rd for each relation projection over table rows: one for Shaw and TXL (AQ), two for DeBERTa (AQ and AK), and none for T5. backward pass is credited twice as much, for its four attention GEMMs and the two gradient GEMMs of each projection. FlashAttention-2 (Dao, 2024) instead credits 2.5 times the forward FLOPs, counting the recomputed scores, which we leave out because not every system recomputes them. Each measurement runs in fresh process with triton.testing.do_bench, which flushes the L2 cache before each sample. After 50ms of warmup, we report the median of at least ten timed runs. Compilation and autotuning happen before timing and are excluded. Systems under torch.compile use its max-autotune mode with static shapes and without CUDA graphs. Within each mechanism and length, the systems run in random order, and we record GPU clocks, power, and temperature instead of locking the clocks. The RTX PRO 6000 and RTX A6000 use the same software as the H200. End-to-end software The speech models run in NeMo 3.0.0 on PyTorch 2.9.1 and CUDA 12.8, and DeBERTa on the software stack of 5.1. Parakeet transcription The test set has 1,155 segments and 11 talks of up to 25 minutes, which we transcribe one at time. We report word error rate (WER) after Whispers text normalization (Radford et al., 2023), for which NVIDIAs model card reports 2.75% (NVIDIA, 2025), and inverse real-time factor (RTFx), the audio seconds processed per wall-clock second. NeMos FlexAttention path captures sequence-length-dependent index arithmetic and bias tensors in its score_mod closure, so each new input length triggers torch.compile recompilation that erases any speedup, and running it uncompiled falls back to much slower unfused implementation. Canary fine-tuning We fine-tune on 100 hours of TEDLIUM 3 training talks, cut into windows of at most 30 seconds and 2, 5, 9, 15, and 18 minutes, for 3 epochs with about 540 seconds of audio per step. Final-epoch training losses match within 0.4% at every window both attentions run. As Whisper does, we decode transcripts that fall into repetition loops again in shorter pieces. From 9-minute windows on, such loops affect one or two long recordings per window, and these recordings account for the remaining WER differences. AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) at learning rate of 2 105, 10% linear warmup, weight decay 0.01, and 16 patents per step in 4K-token micro-batches, and report test accuracy at the best validation epoch. Macro-F1 agrees within 0.3 points from 2K tokens and differs by +1.3 points at 512 tokens. Condevaux & Harispe (2023) report 66.6 micro-F1 and 61.8 macro-F1 for RoBERTa on this task.
